request.prompt:
You are clustering code review findings from the same PR. For each PAIR below, decide whether the two findings describe the SAME underlying issue — same root cause in the same code location. Different wording is fine. A finding about a DIFFERENT defect in the same file or function is NOT the same issue. Severity or aspect differences of the same root cause ARE the same issue.


For THIS scoring pass, duplicate equivalence is stricter than sharing a root cause.
You must compare the COMPLETE MATERIAL CLAIMS, including mechanism, triggering
conditions, execution path, and consequence. The same line or broad concern does
not establish equivalence. A report of wrong-category selection, a case/rename
mismatch, a crash, and a silent fallback are different claims even at one lookup.
An inactive/unbound API concern and an alleged active user-facing failure differ.
A compound report with an additional material claim does NOT equal its subset.
Differences only in wording, severity, or hedging do not create separate claims.
If the claimed mechanisms, triggers or consequences conflict, or one report adds
an unsupported/different material factual claim, return same=false. You are NOT
verifying which claim is true; do not repair or reinterpret either report to make
them match. If unsure whether their full claims are equivalent, return false.

For every numbered pair, extract what A and B actually CLAIM into mechanism,
trigger and consequence. Then list material_differences and give your equivalence
verdict, confidence and reason. same=true requires no material differences.
Return ONLY this JSON object, with EVERY pair index exactly once:
{"pairs":[{"pair":1,"a":{"mechanism":"...","trigger":"...","consequence":"..."},"b":{"mechanism":"...","trigger":"...","consequence":"..."},"material_differences":[],"same":true,"confidence":0.9,"reason":"..."}]}

An admin clicking quickly through the pager sees the wrong member page displayed (page contents and page counter disagree with the actual requested offset) until they click again.

PAIR 16:
A: addMembers has the same defect: the .then calls self.findMembers() without returning it, detaching the reload's failure from the promise chain. After a successful add, a failed refresh leaves the newly added member invisible in the list with no error, so the admin cannot tell whether the add took effect.
B: removeMember and addMembers call self.findMembers() inside .then without returning it, so a failure of the member-list reload is an unhandled promise rejection that leaves the previously rendered member list in place with no error surfaced. After a successful add/remove, if the follow-up findMembers request fails (network drop, 500), the admin still sees the pre-operation member list — e.g. a removed member still appears after a confirmed removal — with no error dialog; the rejection also propagates as an unhandled promise rejection.

PAIR 17:
A: add_members splits the usernames string and issues one User.find_by_username query per username inside the loop (N+1), with no batched WHERE username IN (...) lookup. Adding a large batch of members issues N sequential user lookups plus N group.add association writes instead of a batched load and one save; on an admin action over a big paste this scales linearly per-user at DB roundtrip cost.
B: N+1 query shape in add_members: one SELECT per username plus individual group_user inserts (~2N queries) instead of a single User.where bulk lookup plus bulk insert

PAIR 18:
A: The addMembers action fires this.get("model").addMembers(...) without returning or catching the promise, and never clears the usernames input (the in-code TODO), so a failed PUT is swallowed and the stale names remain in the field. An admin clicks Add, the request fails (network error/500), nothing is added and no error is shown; the input still holds the old names so the next click silently re-submits the same list, compounding the invisible failure.
B: The addMembers action neither returns the model.addMembers promise nor has any in-flight guard or input clearing, so concurrent invocations interleave and the committed input state desyncs from the server. Double-clicking the Add button issues overlapping PUT requests; and because the username input is never cleared after a successful add (the TODO), the same usernames remain in the selector and are re-submitted on the next click, while the controller gives the caller no promise to observe success/failure — a failed add leaves the input populated as if it had been consumed.

PAIR 19:
A: The new <form class="form-horizontal"> wraps the group-name text field and the user-selector input while every button inside it lacks type="button", so pressing Enter in either input performs native form submission. The admin types a group name (or a username in the selector) and presses Enter; the browser submits the form as a GET to the current URL and performs a full page reload, discarding every unsaved edit — name, visibility, alias level — with no save and no error.
B: New <form> wrapper in the admin group template: pressing Enter in the group-name field or user-selector input triggers native implicit form submission to the current URL — a full page reload that discards unsaved edits, since only the save/delete buttons' {{action}} handlers preventDefault

PAIR 20:
A: The per-member template gates the remove link on {{#unless automatic}}, but inside the group-member view the context is the member (a Discourse.User), so 'automatic' resolves against the user record, is undefined, and the link renders for automatic groups too. Admins viewing an automatic group (e.g. admins/moderators) see a working remove icon on each member; clicking it triggers DELETE /admin/groups/:id/members which the server rejects with 422 can_not_modify_automatic, surfacing an error after the fact instead of never offering the action — the old UI correctly disabled member editing for automatic groups.
B: The remove-link guard {{#unless automatic}} is evaluated inside the per-member item view (the sibling bindings {{member.username}}/{{avatar member}} show the context is the member), so 'automatic' resolves against the Discourse.User object — which has no 'automatic' property — instead of the group, and the remove link renders unconditionally. Admins viewing an automatic group (admins/staff/moderators/trust_level_N) see a working-looking remove icon on every member row; confirming the bootbox prompt sends DELETE /admin/groups/:id/members.json which the server rejects with 422, and the unhandled promise rejection surfaces no feedback, so removal appears to silently do nothing.
